• Other names: Pepperwort, Bristly water-clover, Rough water-clover
  • Optimal tank size: 40 litres (10 gallons)
  • Difficulty: easy to medium
  • Lighting: medium to high
  • Optimal pH: 6.0–7.5
  • Optimal GH: 2–12
  • Optimal temperature: 20–25 °C (68–77 °F)
  • Substrate: needed (nutrient-rich)
  • Growth rate: slow to moderate
  • Placement: mostly foreground / midground
  • Height: up to 10 cm
  • CO2: not needed to low
  • Fertilizers: not needed to low
  • Propagation: splitting

Marsilea hirsuta belongs to the family of heterosporous aquatic and semi-aquatic ferns (Marsileaceae). The genus Marsilea comprises about 65 species of aquatic ferns, also known as pepperwort or water clover because of their prominent long-stalked leaves that look like four-leaf clover. The genus was named after Count Luigi Ferdinando Marsilea, an Italian natural scientist.

It is native to Australia. It has also been introduced to parts of Europe and North America in recent times.
Marsilea hirsuta grows mainly in marshes, ponds and floodplains. As an amphibious plant, it can grow either partially or fully submerged in shallow, standing water on sandy or clayey substrates.
A good choice for nano tanks. The minimum tank size is 5 gallons (20 L); the optimal size is 10 gallons (about 40 litres).

One of the easiest plants to care for. It needs no constant pruning, as it is slow-growing and easier to keep than other foreground plants such as Glosso and HC Cuba.

It needs moderate to high lighting to keep a low growth habit and spread horizontally. Avoid low light, which prompts vertical growth and loses the carpeting effect. New or young leaves may be yellowish; after a while they turn their usual green.

Trimming: prune only when the mat gets too dense. Trim the overgrown carpet with scissors and remove the clippings with a net. The first trim may come about two months after planting. Dose a good plant fertilizer regularly (e.g. Seachem Flourish Excel) and do weekly partial water changes.

Planting and propagation

Establish a substrate layer 2.5–5 cm deep. Split clumps into small plantlets with stolons and intact roots; keep them moist (mist with aquarium water or cover with a damp paper towel).

  • With tweezers, hold a plantlet at 40–60 degrees and insert it into the substrate so the root is covered and the shoot is above the substrate.
  • Release the tweezers slowly, wiggling gently to settle the substrate around the plant.
  • Space the other plantlets at least 1–2.5 cm apart for even coverage.

It propagates easily through runners (stolon-like rhizomes lying on the substrate), which spread rapidly and fill empty spaces. Simply split mature rhizomes and replant them.

Alternative: the dry start method also works and shows that the plant suits paludariums. It boosts the development of slow-growing plants and removes algae problems.

Common problems

  • Emersed to submersed: a transition from emersed to submersed form causes melt, and the plant needs time to grow new leaves adapted to the new environment.
  • Vertical growth: caused by low light. With bright light the plant stays compact and spreads horizontally; provide sufficient light and a photoperiod of up to 8 hours daily.
  • Melting: the plant may also melt or stop growing above 26 °C; keep the water at 18–25 °C.
  • Stunted growth: after planting it may show no obvious change for weeks, as the plant uses its energy to anchor.

Temperature: 18–25 °C (64–77 °F). Make sure the water never reaches 26 °C, as it can cause the plant to wither.

pH: 6.0–7.0.

Hardness: tolerates soft to hard water; 4–18 dGH is fine.

Lighting: moderate lighting is ideal, best in the range of 30–60 PAR. Under high light the plant stays smaller. It can survive in low light, but grows slower and a little taller, as if reaching for more light.

CO2: demand is low, so CO2 injection is not mandatory but beneficial; it can significantly improve growth. Regular liquid fertilizer promotes more compact, robust growth.

If you keep shrimp, note that high CO2 levels and copper (present in most fertilizers) are extremely dangerous to shrimp.

Substrate: Marsilea hirsuta requires a nutrient-rich substrate for optimal growth, which helps it form a good carpet. Recommended soils include ADA Amazonia aqua soil, CaribSea Eco-Complete and Seachem Fluorite. In sand or gravel, dose adequate amounts of high-quality fertilizers. Root tabs help with heavy root feeders on any substrate. Substrate depth should be at least 2.5–5 cm for better anchorage.

Marsilea hirsuta is a small, perennial, creeping plant with thin stems, each bearing a compound frond divided into two, three or four leaflets, in a low form once fully settled. It has dark or lime-green blades up to 1 cm long and 5 mm wide; the leaves are circinate.

The plant is compact and can reach up to 10 cm. In low light it grows taller, while under high light it tends to stay smaller. It forms a long, slender, creeping rhizome often bearing small pale brown hairs, and produces numerous runners that spread rapidly across the base of the tank.

Unlike Marsilea quadrifolia, which produces floating leaves that reach the water surface, Marsilea hirsuta stays permanently submerged and produces no floating leaves.

It also reproduces by spores, which is more common in its emersed form. Being heterosporous, it produces two different kinds of spores that can remain dormant for long periods to survive unfavourable conditions.

Benefits

  • Aquascape: a great choice for aquascapes (particularly Iwagumi); an excellent ground-cover plant that forms dense, beautiful carpets.
  • Shelter: the carpet is a good spawning medium for egg scatterers and provides shelter for bottom-dwelling fish, fry and shrimp.
  • Foraging place: a foraging ground for shrimp and snails; biofilm grows on it, an ideal first food for newly hatched fry and shrimplets.
  • Oxygenation: helps oxygenate and filter the water through photosynthesis.

Tankmates

Best kept with small, peaceful community fish such as bleeding heart tetra, neon tetra, mollies, killifish, swordtails, white cloud mountain minnows, zebra danio, cherry barb, sunburst platy, Endler's livebearers, otocinclus and pygmy corydoras.

Shrimp: choose species that prefer the same water parameters (mostly pH), for example crystal red shrimp, blue bolt shrimp, Caridina cf. babaulti.

Snails: ornamental snails should not be kept long in low-pH water as it harms their shells. If pH is close to 7.0, almost any snail or dwarf shrimp can be kept, e.g. Japanese trapdoor snails, ramshorn snails, nerite snails, Malaysian trumpet snails, black devil snails, Asolene spixi, rabbit snails.

Avoid species that may eat Marsilea hirsuta, such as koi, goldfish, oscars, rainbowfish, Jack Dempsey, clown loaches and African cichlids. Most crayfish and freshwater crabs are not a good combination either, as they cut, eat and uproot everything in the tank.

Buying and quarantine

The plant is readily available in pet stores and from reputable online vendors, and is very affordable. Choose healthy, vibrant specimens with sufficient roots.

Quarantine any new plants before adding them to the tank. They can carry parasites, pests such as snails, or even predators (dragonfly and damselfly nymphs, etc.). They may also have been treated with pesticides, which are extremely poisonous to fish, shrimp and other invertebrates.
